title: Hi, what's your name?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, say your name, ask how someone is, and see for yourself that Finnish has no articles and no grammatical gender.
bekal: greet with *hei*, *moi*, *hyvää päivää*, and *hyvää iltaa*, each in its proper place
say your name with *minun nimeni on* and *olen*, and ask other people theirs
put together the six forms of the verb *olla* — the only verb you truly must memorize in this unit

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ensimmäinen päivä kielikurssilla
dialogs.intro: First day of a language course at a university in Helsinki. Two new students sit next to each other before class begins.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hei! Minun nimeni on Budi. Entä sinä?
lines.id: Hi! My name is Budi. And you?
lines.literal: hi! my name-my is Budi. and you?

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.id: I'm Aino. Nice to meet you!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ihan hyvää, kiitos. Oletko sinä suomalainen?
lines.id: Pretty good, thanks. Are you Finnish?
lines.literal: quite good, thanks. are-? you Finnish?

lines.text: Joo, minä olen Tampereelta. Oletko sinä opiskelija?

notes: **Hei works both ways, and repeating it means goodbye.** The same word covers "hi" and "bye"; doubled (*hei hei*, *moi moi*), it always means goodbye — not an extra-warm hello. Danish and Swedish work exactly the same way, and it's the opposite of what most people guess.

**Mikä sinun nimesi on** marks ownership twice.** Literally "what **your** name-**your** is": *sinun* (your) in front, and the ending *-si* (your) on *nime-*. Finnish deliberately locks it in twice, and in casual speech the front one is often dropped: *Mikä nimesi on?* The ending can never go.

**Mitä kuuluu** literally means "what is heard".** Not "how are you". So the answer is about the news, not about you: *kiitos, hyvää* — "thanks, good". Note the order: Finns almost always put *kiitos* **first**, and that sounds far more natural than the reverse.

**There isn't a single article in this whole dialogue.** No "a", no "the", and no gender for nouns. *Opiskelija* means "student", "a student", and "the student" all at once. This isn't a textbook simplification; Finnish simply has neither.

**Oletko** — questions are made by attaching **-ko/-kö**.** There's no helper word like English "do". The verb moves to the front and takes the ending: *sinä olet* (you are) → *oletko sinä?* (are you?). The same ending is at work in *puhutko* and *ymmärrätkö*.

**Joo and kyllä both mean "yes".** *Joo* is casual and heard far more often; *kyllä* is a bit firmer or more formal. For "no" there's *ei* — and this *ei* isn't just a word but a **verb** that changes form. That surprise is saved for Unit 7.

grammars.title: Olla — the verb "to be"
body: The first verb you must master, and the only one in this unit that is truly irregular. The good news: after *olla*, almost every other verb follows a tidy pattern.
after: ⚠️ **Hän is one word for both he and she.** Finnish makes no distinction at all. Many Finns mix up "he" and "she" in English for life for exactly this reason — and you get to skip the choice entirely.

For things, use *se* ("it"), not *hän*: *Se on kirja* — it's a book. In casual speech Finns actually use *se* for people too, but don't copy that until you know when it sounds friendly and when it sounds rude.

**The pronoun can be dropped** for *minä*, *sinä*, *me*, and *te*, because the verb ending already says who it is: *olen opiskelija* can only mean "I'm a student". But *hän* and *he* can **not** be dropped — the forms *on* and *ovat* don't tell you who is meant.

grammars.title: Asking with -ko / -kö
body: Finnish has no question helper like "do" or "is it". The word being asked about moves to the front of the sentence and takes a question ending.
after: Choose **-ko** or **-kö** by vowel harmony: *oletko* (back-vowel word) but *ymmärrätkö* (front-vowel word). It's exactly the rule from the pronunciation chapter.
If there's a question word (*mikä*, *mitä*, *kuka*, *missä*), the *-ko* ending is **not used**: *Mikä sinun nimesi on?* — not *mikäko*.

Whatever goes first decides what is being asked. *Oletko sinä opiskelija?* asks about the status; *Sinäkö olet opiskelija?* asks about the person — "is it **you** who's the student?". Same ending, different emphasis.

blocks.text: Finnish picks its greeting by the time of day and by how close you are to the other person. Getting it wrong isn't a grammar mistake but a mood mistake — and that's actually more noticeable.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Hyvää päivää* sounds more formal than it looks. To a friend your age it feels stiff, like saying "good afternoon" to your roommate. To a cashier, a doctor, or an official, it's just right.

blocks.title: One Finnish habit worth knowing first
items: Silence isn't awkwardness. Long pauses in a conversation are considered normal and polite — they give the other person room to think. Don't rush to fill them out of reflex.
On the other hand, interrupting is considered far ruder than in many other countries. Wait until the other person has really finished, even if the pause feels long.

blocks.text: The ten phrases below aren't grammar to study — they're an emergency kit. Memorize them whole now; understand how they're built later.
*Ole hyvä* literally means "be good", and it's used for two things: answering a thank-you, and handing something to someone. To several people the form is *olkaa hyvä*.

blocks.title: One sentence that changes your experience of Finland
items: *Voidaanko puhua suomea? Minä opiskelen.* — "Could we speak Finnish? I'm learning."

The classic problem for Finnish learners isn't unfriendly people but the opposite: the moment they hear your accent, almost every Finn automatically switches to English to be helpful — and their English is excellent. The sentence above stops that politely, and nearly everyone will happily stay in Finnish.

blocks.text: The "possessive" column gets full use in Unit 4; for now, just recognize *minun* and *sinun*, which already appeared in the dialogue.

⚠️ **Te has two jobs.** It's "you all" and also the polite "you" to one person, just like French *vous*. But Finns use it far less than the French or Germans do: with cashiers, coworkers, often even the boss, Finns simply say *sinä*. Save *te* for much older people or truly formal situations.

In everyday speech, *minä* often shrinks to *mä* and *sinä* to *sä*: *mä oon*, *sä oot*. You'll hear it everywhere in Helsinki. This course uses the standard forms, because they're understood everywhere, while the casual forms vary from region to region.

Choose the right greeting. Write your answer as one word or one phrase.
items: You walk into a bakery at eight in the morning. To the baker you say ____.
You run into a classmate in the cafeteria at eleven. You say ____.

You say goodbye to a classmate, casually. You say ____.
